Targeted enforcement at identified domestic bushmeat market hotspots will cause subsequent international scale seizures to show reduced genetic assignment probability to those hotspots and increased assignment to adjacent, less-patrolled regions in a multi-year time series.

Domestic bushmeat markets in identified trafficking hotspots serve as recruitment sources for international scale trade, such that the geographic origin profiles of pangolins in long-range markets predict the origin profiles of subsequent international seizures within a six-month window.

Genetically assigned pangolin trafficking hotspots are temporally dynamic, such that intensified enforcement in southwestern Cameroon, southwestern Borneo, and Myanmar will cause a measurable shift in the geographic provenance of seizures to alternative source populations within 24 months.

Repeated temporal genomic assignment of domestic bushmeat markets and international seizures will reveal that the shared sourcing hotspots in Cameroon for white-bellied pangolins shift synchronously over time, indicating that domestic bushmeat markets can serve as early sentinel systems for emerging international trafficking source regions.

If domestic bushmeat markets and international seizures in pangolin trafficking hotspots draw from the same harvesting networks, then internationally seized individuals will share significantly more mitochondrial haplotypes and first-order kin relationships with conspecifics sold in nearby long-range bushmeat markets than with individuals from field-sampled reference populations in the same region.

As enforcement pressure increases in domestic market hotspots that also supply international scale trade, subsequent international pangolin seizures will show a temporal shift in predicted geographic origin toward adjacent regions, indicating adaptive rerouting of trafficking networks.
